draft.title: GNI per person
card: Gross national income (GNI) is the total income earned by a country's people and businesses in a year, including income they earn from other countries.
GNI per person is GNI divided by the number of people. It shows the average income in a country.
It is an average, so it does not show how fairly income is shared. A few very rich people can raise it while many others stay poor.
It also says nothing directly about health or education. Two countries with the same GDP per person can differ in both.
draft.remember: GNI per person is an average income. It hides sharing, health and education.

a.q: What does GNI per person show about a country?
opts: Its average income for each person
How equally income is shared among people
How long people in it usually live
How many children go to school in it
a.why: GNI per person divides total national income by the population, which gives an average income. It cannot show how income is shared, because an average hides differences between people.
a.clue: Think of what you get when you divide a total by the number of people.

b.q: In ten years, Country R's GNI per person rose sharply. The mine owners live in Country R, so their extra income counts in its GNI. Almost all the gain went to them, and most workers earned no more. How is this possible?
opts: It is an average, so a few large gains can lift it
It shows the income of a typical worker in a country
It measures health and schooling as well as income
It divides GNI by the number of workers, not people
b.why: GNI per person is an average, so big gains for a few people can raise it even when most incomes stay flat. It is tempting to think it shows a typical worker's income, but an average hides how income is spread, which is why it rose here while most workers gained nothing.
b.clue: What happens to an average when a few values grow a lot?

a.best: Its average income for each person

b.best: It is an average, so a few large gains can lift it
